chapters.t: The Tale of the Elephant and the Crocodile
chapters.s: In this chapter, an elephant of the village is caught in a crocodile’s grip in Jori Pokhari, and the villagers save him by bringing the ancient tale of Gajendra-Moksha together with their own local tradition. From here onward, the term “Gaja-Graha” will recur repeatedly in the later part of the story. That night, as promised, the villagers made a special offering to the Original Crocodile. Then Budhba addressed the village: “Today you saw that an ancient tale and our local tradition are different forms of the same…
chapters.g: Chapter -69 joins the celebrated Gajendra-Moksha story of the Bhagavata Purana with the local mythic-folk tradition of the “Original Crocodile,” showing how a great classical narrative and a local oral tradition can express the same deep human truth in different languages.…

chapters.s: In this chapter a new formal court enters the village’s system of justice—and with it is sown the seed of a new, slow hunger that much later will be known as the “Ghost of the Court.” Bhola’s case was finally decided after five years—in his favour. By then, however, his field had been ruined for years and his children had grown up hungry.…
chapters.g: Chapter -68 places an acutely relevant modern social problem within a historical setting: procedural delay in the justice system, the reality behind the principle “justice delayed is justice denied.” The chapter clearly plants the narrative seed of the “Ghost of the Court” in Parts 1 and 2—the creature that feeds on “date after date” and is said to be more dangerous than a crocodile.…

chapters.s: In this chapter, for the first time, a labour recruiter arrives at the village gate selling dreams of work in distant lands—and Budhba faces a new question: how can he witness a name that has left the village and travelled far away? With the birth of this custom, Garh Narikel’s tradition of memory began for the first time to think beyond its geographical boundaries. It accepted that in the future the village’s children would travel to distant…
chapters.g: Chapter -67 offers an early evocation of the colonial “girmitiya” system of indentured labour, under which thousands of workers from Bihar and elsewhere in India—often exploited through illiteracy and poverty—were taken to distant colonies such as Mauritius, Fiji, and the Caribbean, and many never returned.…

chapters.s: In this chapter the informal women’s platform inherited from Phulesari takes formal shape for the first time as “The Women’s Night Assembly,” a name that will reappear much later in Part 1. In time the Night Assembly became a permanent part of village life, moving alongside the official court and filling its gaps. Much later, in the modern age, it would change its form and take a new name…
chapters.g: Chapter -66 gives narrative form to an important social and institutional development: when a formal, largely male-dominated justice system cannot adequately address women’s particular experiences and needs, women often develop parallel systems of justice—informal, yet socially powerful.…

chapters.s: In this chapter, for the first time, someone misuses Budhba’s name—and the village must answer a new question: how can one distinguish a true witness from a false claim? The incident became known in village memory as “The Procession of the False Ghost,” a cautionary tale told to every new generation: “Whoever claims to be a witness but asks for money is not a witness; he is a thief.”
chapters.g: Chapter -65 addresses a universal social problem: when a true and respected spiritual or cultural tradition becomes famous, opportunists arise who imitate it in order to exploit the innocent financially. Budhba’s simple test—“a true witness never asks for money”—offers a practical, universally applicable defence against spiritual exploitation.…

chapters.s: In this chapter, the land of the leatherworkers’ quarter is threatened once again, just as it was in Sukhdev Mahato’s time. But this time the village has new weapons in its hands. “No, Champavati,” Budhba said softly. “No struggle is wasted if its memory remains alive. That is why I have kept witness all these years…
chapters.g: Chapter -64 brings one strand of the narrative cycle to a meaningful completion. The theme of land injustice that began with Sukhdev Mahato’s tragedy in Chapter -92 now produces the opposite outcome, because centuries of accumulated community capacity—literacy, documentation, legal knowledge, and women’s solidarity—have changed what is possible.…

chapters.t: The First Page from the Press
chapters.s: In this chapter, the first printing press opens in a town near the village—and, many generations later, a descendant of Haripati tries to fulfil an unfinished ancestral dream through a new technology. Meanwhile, in his town press, Gangadhar printed several other small village books—the curriculum of the Coconut-Leaf School, the rules of the Women’s Night Assembly…
chapters.g: Chapter -63 marks an important technological transition: the arrival of printing, which brought a revolutionary change in the history of Indian-language literature. Budhba’s decision not to print the story yet, but to let it remain living and developing, is an interesting example of the narrative cycle’s own self-awareness: the story itself knows that it is not yet complete.…

chapters.s: In this chapter, under British rule, a terrible famine strikes—and the village must learn the difference between sitting in expectation of government help and organising itself. Hearing this, Budhba said proudly, “Savitridevi, today you have proved the lesson I have tried to teach for hundreds of years: to bear witness and to wait are two different things.…
chapters.g: Chapter -62 touches the historical complexity of famine management in colonial India, where government relief policy, however orderly it appeared on paper, often proved inadequate in practice because of bureaucratic delay and geographical distance. The chapter emphasises the power of community self-reliance and mutual aid, showing how social capital accumulated over centuries—organisational capacity, shared resources…

chapters.s: In this chapter, an extraordinary comet appears in the sky—and the frightened villagers ask Budhba what calamity it foretells. That night Budhba moved through Channa Grove touching every tree—if “touching” is the right word for a being whose touch is itself a shadow—deep in thought.…
chapters.g: Chapter -61 uses the appearance of a comet—historically interpreted in many cultures of the world as an evil omen—to prepare the ground for the next phase of the story. Budhba’s rational but cautious response—the star itself is not to blame, yet vigilance is necessary—offers a balanced path between superstition and complete dismissal.…

chapters.s: One month after the comet disappears, the most terrible fire in the village’s history breaks out—and Channa Grove itself is placed in danger. The villagers rebuilt the burned houses, this time more safely than before: special places for lamps, emergency stores of water, and new rules for fire safety.…
chapters.g: Chapter -60 demonstrates the power of collective action, especially during a large natural or human-made disaster. Forming a human chain to carry water is a real and historically effective emergency technique used by organised communities. Budhba’s role is important here: he does not miraculously extinguish the fire himself; he gives direction, while the actual work is accomplished through collective human effort.…

chapters.s: After the fire, the rainy season becomes unusually fierce—and the Kamala-Balan, after many years, again breaks its bounds. Budhba answered with deep contentment, “Indrani, this is the greatest gift for me—to see that my memory, over time, has become knowledge in your hands that saves lives, not merely names.”
chapters.g: Chapter -59 turns an important principle of disaster management into narrative: an early-warning system and a predetermined evacuation plan, however simple—here, a drum rhythm and pre-identified safe ground—can dramatically reduce disaster mortality. Compared with the first flood in Chapter -89, this chapter gives clear, measurable evidence of the village’s accumulated institutional learning…

chapters.s: After fire and flood, the comet’s third and final warning is fulfilled: a new water-borne disease arises from the foul standing water left by the flood. The story of the three disasters of that year remained in village memory as “the Year of Three Calamities.” At every new-moon kabaddi, along with the names of those lost that year, one sentence began to be spoken…
chapters.g: Chapter -58 completes the three-level disaster sequence that began in Chapters -61 and -60—the comet’s omen, fire, and flood—with water-borne disease. This is epidemiologically realistic, because outbreaks of water-borne disease after flooding are a well-known phenomenon.…

chapters.s: After the Year of Three Calamities, an English scholar comes to study the village traditions—but even with good intentions, his writing fails to understand the story accurately. Nandkishor wrote Thompson Sahib a courteous but firm letter explaining the true meaning of the village traditions. No reply came. But continuing the line of Gangadhar and Haripati Kavi…
chapters.g: Chapter -57 touches a real and documented tendency in colonial-era ethnographic study: British scholars, often with good intentions, studied Indian folk traditions, yet cultural bias could lead them to portray local knowledge systems and social arrangements as “primitive” or “superstitious.” The chapter emphasises the importance of self-representation—the principle that a community must write its own story in its own language…

chapters.s: In this chapter, the wave of the freedom movement reaches Garh Narikel—and the village discovers that the art of collective organisation learned over centuries is equally useful in the struggle for freedom. That evening Budhba said to Lakshmidevi, “Today I saw a new kind of kabaddi—a game in which every villager played against an unseen opponent for the sake of self-respect and kept every name safe without losing one.”
chapters.g: Chapter -56 shows how community capacities developed over centuries—shared decision-making, dissemination of information, and patient resistance—can also be applied effectively to a large political struggle such as the freedom movement. The Gandhian principle of satyagraha—nonviolent yet resolute resistance—naturally resonates with the village’s own long traditions, such as its encounter with Amil Jay Singh in Chapter -85.…
